title: When Does a Quantum Speedup Survive End-to-End?
authors: Pablo Herrero Gómez, Antonio Jimeno Morenilla, David Muñoz Hernández, Higinio Mora Mora
abstract: Primitive quantum speedups are interface-relative: they depend on the input access used to run the primitive and on the output contract used to consume its state or samples. This paper introduces a transcript-level admissibility relation \(A_M\preceq_{\mathrm{int}}A_Q\), defined relative to the declared implementation package of the quantum interface. It identifies which adaptive classical access transcripts that same package licenses, with all setup, transcript-generation, and precision overheads charged.   The main application is an operational audit for normalized-Betti estimation in clique-complex TDA, separating three declared-interface regimes. Reversible indexed simplex interfaces certify matched classical simplex sampling and local Laplacian row access by evaluating their reversible routines on single computational branches. Membership-based preparations induce a rejection route of overhead \(\binom{n}{k+1}/|S_k|\). Abstract spectral or block-encoding interfaces require an accompanying implementation package, transcript reduction, or shared representation. Under the indexed certificate and interface closure, the end-to-end cost is fixed by the imported estimator's spectral dependence on the gap \(γ\); the concretely realized bounded-treewidth family already admits exact \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\) classical Betti computation by rank over \(\mathbb{Q}\). A low-rank separation supports the role of access and output contracts.
summary: This paper develops a rigorous theoretical framework to determine if a claimed quantum speedup survives when all practical overheads, including input access and output requirements, are accounted for. By introducing an 'interface-admissibility' audit, it provides a formal method to compare quantum algorithms against a matched classical baseline, showing that the advantage is highly dependent on the specific computational context.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental question of when a quantum computational speedup remains valid when considering the entire end-to-end process, which is shown to be dependent on the specific input access and output contract.
main_result: It establishes a formal framework, the admissibility relation, to audit quantum claims by comparing them against a rigorously defined, interface-closed classical baseline, showing that the advantage is highly context-dependent.
method: The authors introduce an interface-admissibility relation and an 'interface audit' procedure to formally charge all setup, transcript-generation, and precision overheads associated with matching classical and quantum access models.
model_or_system: The framework is highly abstract, dealing with general quantum access models ($	ext{AQ}$), classical access models ($	ext{AM}$), and output contracts ($	ext{O}$). It is applied specifically to the operational audit of normalized-Betti estimation in Topological Data Analysis (TDA) for clique-complexes.
key_observables: Quantum speedup, Betti numbers, end-to-end cost ($	ext{T}_{	ext{E2E}}$), and overheads ($\Gamma_M$).
important_parameters: The gap $\gamma$ (spectral dependence), the structure of the declared implementation package ($	ext{IQ}(x)$), and the nature of the output contract (e.g., scalar vs. dense vector).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the explicit definition and certification of the interface-admissibility relation and the assumption that the comparison must use an 'interface-closed' classical baseline.
figures_summary: The notes reference a narrative map (Table 1) summarizing the framework components and a canonical case summary (Table 4) comparing various tasks (e.g., TDA Betti, QPCA) across different contracts and regimes.
paper_structure: The paper develops a general framework for auditing quantum claims by defining the admissibility relation, applying this audit to specific physical problems like TDA, and concluding with a summary table comparing various computational tasks.
why_interesting: While the application is TDA, the underlying methodology—creating a rigorous, overhead-aware comparison between quantum and classical complexity—is a foundational theoretical tool relevant to assessing quantum advantage in any physical simulation or computation.
